near_miss.why_not: Russian adjective plus genitive beverage contrasts with Latvian genitive medutiņa plus abstract saldumiņu in a marriage sweetness/bitterness contrast. Both lexical families are cognate, but sweetness is inherent in honey; late witnesses and different syntax do not establish an inherited poetic formula. Wider search finds Homeric μέθυ ἡδύ and Vedic sweet Soma, retained separately as a search lead.

Serbian royal metaphor and Russian decorated interior differ from the Latvian falling star; celestial location and luminosity are ordinary attributes, not distinctive common wording. Pindar describes lightning, not stars.
Russian movement between hills versus Latin hills transmitting an echo: different semantic roles and contexts; repeated landscape noun alone is inadequate.
Russian sleep/lie pairing and Norse lying down in bed and sleeping are routine narrative actions; Latin covers the eyes with sleep and provides no corresponding cognate construction.

Serbian ravens eat battlefield corpses; Atharvavedic examples concern healing and directing demons to eat their own flesh. Cognate eat + flesh is basic dietary language, without matching distinctive figure or ritual context. Sanskrit epic moral condemnation is different again.
Russian boot-toe or arrow extremity versus Latin wasting human nose in plague; only the anatomical metaphor is comparable and the remaining wording and context differ.
Serbian courage and resolve versus Irish Congal overwhelmed by madness and a demonic fury; no shared epithet or construction beyond heart, and the Irish passage has classical learned colouring.
Serbian igniting a gun versus Vedic goat/fire identification or fever invocation. The slab does not show an equivalent living-fire collocation in the Vedic passages.
Serbian oath by firm faith and Cato seller swearing true performance differ in formula and legal function. Common oath language cannot establish phrase inheritance.
Same natural kinship relation but no marked formula; marriage estrangement in Latvian and threatened return to maternal kin in Serbian can arise independently.
Russian lowering eyes in dejection versus Homeric dying men striking earth with forehead: distinct verbs, body parts and narrative functions.
Russian fourth three-year service period versus Latvian fourth year. Counting is not inherited phraseology.
Serbian gun thunders; Norse stanza has noise of steel but its cited passage concerns combat and wolf over corpses. Old English grim is not a thunder verb. No matching cognate collocation.
Russian erotic quill/inkwell metaphor versus Lucretius counterfactual inheritance of bird colours: feather and swan are not shared in the same syntactic relation.

near_miss.why_not: Norse partner is about not washing hands or combing hair before vengeance: kembði is not a tooth and bál is a pyre, not an adjective meaning white. Greek corpus search finds λευκῷ ὀδόντι (Od. 21.219, 23.74) and λευκὸν ὀδόντα (Il. 11.416), but neither member is cognate with Serbian bijel + zub; natural tooth colour and differing human/boar contexts do not justify a reconstructed formula.

Root pairing is real: тёшутъ, дерева against τέκτονα δούρων and τέχνῃ with δουρός. Russian has hewing a maple-wood coffin for a named dead person, not an explicit verb-object formula for poetic creation; Greek has a literal carpenter, a craft simile, or metaphorical spear craft. Corpus search confirms literal woodworking as the semantic baseline. The noun/verb syntactic mismatch and normal selection of material prevent an inheritance claim.
Russian дологъ agrees with день, the duration slept through; Avestan darəγō concerns long sleeping in a demon’s exhortation. Ordinary duration, different syntax and no distinctive shared setting.
Russian light clouds in the eyes, while Catullus speaks of eyes growing faint in the following context line. No shared cognate collocation beyond a broad physiological metaphor.

Serbian снијежне јабуке is an erotic breast metaphor; Irish ublaib/uball concern apples caught on hair, while gilithir snechta predicates whiteness of súile, eyes. Thus apples and snow are not collocated in the Irish description. gilithir is the equative of gel, as white as; the other Irish passage throws an apple and has no snow comparison.

Russian personifies the wolf as овчиникъ, a sheepskin worker, expanded by stripping skins. Vedic wolf/sheep predation similes and Greek sheep among wolves lack that occupational figure. Shared ecological opposition and two inherited animal names are insufficient; morphology and syntactic roles differ.

Serbian mora slana and Old English brim ... sealt describe the sea’s ordinary salinity; only salt is cognate. Serbian obala is shore, not a verb corresponding to weallan. Insufficient distinctive wording or congruent figure.

Cognate colour root and Balto-Slavic hand noun are real; Serbian hands seized and bound versus Lithuanian hand given in a wedding context. Late records and widespread unmarked body-part epithet do not separate inheritance from independent convention or regional transmission.

near_miss.lead: neither day nor night has rest
near_miss.why_not: Two cognate elements (night and rest), with renewed day word, form a real semantic parallel. Russian distress over separation contrasts with Plautine labour; neither/nor day/night is a transparent exhaustive merism and no rarer shared framing establishes inheritance. Wider search finds a Norse narrative equivalent but adds no early independent ritual or poetic context.
Russian smoke from a horse or dust of travel and Lucretian volcanic smoke share a motion metaphor, but smoke billows naturally; source, syntax and accompanying imagery do not match closely enough.
The Russian verb is Розгорелось, split by OCR; лось is not elk. Thus comparison to Homeric stag-heart is artificial. The actual anger-as-heat motif is too broad to claim from this bundle.

Russian ночныхъ modifies татей; Vedic thieves are a comparison for stars departing with nights before the sun. Thief is cognate, but nights is not an epithet of thieves and Russian has no dawn/star simile. No inherited phrase demonstrated.
Russian seasonal succession versus Vedic enumerated seasons in a longevity blessing and Latin agricultural timing. Calendar sequence alone is not a distinctive merism or shared formula.

Serbian swan feathers and Russian quill or feather-light club compare with Lucretius white raven feathers and counterfactual black swans in separate clauses. No shared swan-feather collocation in the Latin.

Serbian sleep overtakes a child on a stone; Irish Scáthach gives Cú Chulainn a sleep potion (deog suaín, genitive singular of súan) to keep him from battle. Sleep is cognate but there is no shared wording for the mechanism.

Serbian doing honour and Greek honouring or holding in honour have related honour vocabulary but are ordinary social expressions; predicates and construction differ and no distinctive shared formula occurs.
Russian star rolls across sky in relation to locating Churilo, Latvian star falls into sea. Star and sky location are insufficient; motion verbs, destination and story differ.

Same mismatch as BS-29a65: Vedic jīvatā does not qualify agni. Wider root-pair search returns living humans near fire and philosophical identification of fire with life, not the Serbian ignition phrase.
Same rejection as BS-0b015: Russian locomotion versus Lucretius hills relaying echoes, with no distinctive shared syntax beyond noun repetition.
Same rejection as BS-36d7b: ordinary kinship expression in related marriage settings, without evidence distinguishing ancient formula from regional or independent usage.
Ordinary year numbering; Norse fourth letter in BS-e92f4 is additionally not a year. No distinctive inherited context.

Same comparison to Latvian BV 26844 already rejected under BS-00790: literal Russian beverage versus abstract sweetness of a prospective spouse, ordinary honey sweetness and late sources. Repetition supports Russian formulaicity, not cross-branch inheritance by itself.

search_lead.cognate: Russian меду and Greek μέθυ continue *médʰu. Russian сладкий and Greek ἡδύ are not an exact cognate adjective pair; sweetness is semantically matched through renewal.
search_lead.argument: Both are noun plus sweet epithet in convivial consumption, and the Greek phrase recurs formulaically. This is a better syntactic and contextual partner than the Latvian abstract sweetness in the slab. Wine in Greek versus honey drink in Russian represents beverage drift. Late Russian transmission and inherent sweetness remain serious reasons to withhold an inheritance claim.

search_lead.cognate: Russian ночь ~ Norse nótt; Russian покой ~ Norse hvíld at the root *kʷyeh₁-. Day is renewed.
search_lead.argument: Both deny rest through the exhaustive day/night cycle. The Norse army is ordered not to rest at night any more than by day, unlike Russian emotional distress; this excluded-layer medieval witness is a comparative lead only, not evidence by itself of inherited poetic wording.
